arch-002.title: The carbon cycle takes its basic form
arch-002.text: Early carbon isotope ratios look much like today's. That suggests the carbon cycle's basic features were in place as early as about 4 Ga. Much of the young atmosphere's carbon dioxide dissolved in water and reacted with calcium and magnesium from weathered rock, building carbonate sediments. In the cycle, carbon is stored for very long periods as limestone or fossil fuels. Plate tectonics keeps rearranging the continents, which moves carbon dioxide to and from the large continental carbonate stores.

arch-004.title: The Napier mountains rise in Antarctica
arch-004.text: Some of Earth's first metamorphic rocks may have formed in East Antarctica. Mountain building raised the Napier range there, dated to 4000 ± 200 Ma, and its faulting and folding may have produced them. Metamorphism most commonly happens deep in the crust, where buried rocks undergo intense changes in temperature and pressure during mountain building. One source places the start of the orogeny at the beginning of the Archean.

arch-066.title: Microbes begin to burn sulfur
arch-066.text: Some microbes make a living from sulfur. Microbial sulfur oxidation is a process in which microorganisms oxidize reduced sulfur compounds to get energy, often supporting carbon fixation by autotrophs. The earliest evidence, about 2.52 Ga, comes from South Africa's Gamohaan Formation. It shows sulfur-oxidizing bacteria evolved before the Great Oxidation Event. Only bacteria and archaea oxidize reduced sulfur compounds.

prot-009.title: The Dhala impact in India
prot-009.text: An impact struck the Bundelkhand craton and left the largest impact structure in India. Its size is uncertain: some sources estimate a diameter of 3 km, others 11 km. Its age is also poorly constrained. The Dhala impact is estimated to have occurred between 2.44 and 2.24 Ga.

prot-011.title: Dike swarms cut Scotland and Australia
prot-011.text: Rifting left its marks as swarms of dikes, sheets of rock that cut across older crust. The Scourie dike swarm cut Scotland's Lewisian gneisses, overlapping the Inverian deformation at the start of the Proterozoic. Around 2410 Ma the Widgiemooltha swarm intruded the Yilgarn Craton, close in time to the Sebanga Poort dike in Zimbabwe. These intrusions in Northwestern Europe, South Africa and Australia are tied to the rifting of Kenorland. Yet Kenorland moved little, and there are no signs an ocean developed.

prot-028.title: The Glenburgh orogeny joins Pilbara and Yilgarn
prot-028.text: Western Australia was stitched together in a collision. The Pilbara Craton and the Glenburgh Terrane collided with the Yilgarn craton, bringing substantial granite magmatism and intense deformation and metamorphism to the Glenburgh Terrane. That collision created the Errabiddy Shear Zone. Between 1990 and 2004 some geologists proposed instead that the orogeny came from the Yilgarn and Pilbara cratons colliding.

prot-031.title: The early Ruker orogeny shapes Antarctica
prot-031.text: Much of Antarctica was assembled in one mountain-building event. The early Ruker orogeny was a key step in the continent's assembly, adding much of central Antarctica to the nucleus in East Antarctica. It also joined East Antarctica to an unknown continental block as Columbia formed. Many of the rocks were deformed and metamorphosed close to the end of the orogeny, around 1.7 billion years ago.

prot-052.title: The Oklo natural nuclear reactors
prot-052.text: In what is now Oklo, Gabon, nature ran nuclear reactors. Concentrated uranium deposits started reacting after groundwater flooded them. The reactions ran on and off, probably never above 100 kilowatts. Analysis of isotope ratios of uranium, of the fission products and of their stable daughter nuclides confirmed it. Groundwater-moderated natural reactors are not thought to have been possible before the early photosynthesizers began producing oxygen on a planetary scale.

prot-056.title: The Shoemaker impact structure
prot-056.text: In the Mid West of Western Australia an impact left shatter cones and shocked quartz across a structure at least 30 km wide. Its age is uncertain, and researchers disagree. The most cited age, about 1,630 Ma, records a reheating of the granite that may be the impact or only a regional tectonic event. K-Ar dating gives ages as young as 568 ± 20 Ma, which could also date the impact or tectonic activity. The idea of an impact was first published in 1974.

prot-057.title: The earliest red algae
prot-057.text: India's Vindhya Range holds the oldest known red algae. The Chitrakoot Formation preserves Rafatazmia and Ramathallus, and the oldest known red algal mats date to about 1.6 Ga. Rafatazmia chitrakootensis is a filamentous alga described from dolomite in central India. Its cells have been said to resemble oscillatoriacean cyanobacteria and probably multicellular red algae. The find pushes the age of the oldest red alga back by about 400 million years, to about 1,650 ± 89 (2σ) million years ago.

prot-064.title: The Volyn biota of Ukraine
prot-064.text: Tiny fossils survived in rock cavities. About 1.5 Ga, exceptionally preserved microfossils formed in cavities of igneous rocks in what is now Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine. Precambrian fossils are usually poorly preserved, but these cavities held silicon tetrafluoride-rich fluids that favored fossilization. The Volyn samples came from miarolitic pegmatites of the Korosten Pluton in the Ukrainian Shield. They include filaments of varied shapes and fungus-like organisms, possibly among the first fossils of the deep biosphere.

prot-074.title: The Musgrave orogeny in central Australia
prot-074.text: Heat from deep in the mantle reshaped central Australia. Between 1.22 and 1.12 Ga three orogenic events shaped the Musgrave Province, a 220,000 km² region formed via a magma plume. The Musgravian orogeny about 1,200 Ma melted the lower crust and produced the voluminous Kulgera granites. It is read as an intracontinental orogeny caused by significant upwelling of heat and material from the mantle. The Musgrave Block is mainly exposed through the Petermann Orogeny at about 535-550 Ma, which exhumed the belt along the Woodroffe Thrust.

prot-077.title: The Stac Fada impact and its missing crater
prot-077.text: The crater is missing, but the debris is not. The Stac Fada Member records an impact about 1.2 Ga, and its inferred crater, about 40 km wide, has not been found. The member is an impactite, a mixture of suevite and clast-poor impact melt rocks. It is exposed along about 50 km of the Wester Ross coast, from Loch Ewe in the south to the Stoer peninsula in the north. The impact was in the near vicinity, likely in the Minch or near Lairg.

prot-082.title: The Nonesuch lake fossils
prot-082.text: An oxygenated lake in the Midcontinent Rift preserved freshwater microbes exceptionally well in what is now Michigan. Its shale, siltstone and sandstone are 150–210 m thick and extend from Michigan and Wisconsin to Iowa. The Nonesuch beds contain common organic carbon and pyrite. The shale has enough organic carbon (greater than 0.5%) to be a potential petroleum source bed, but exploration wells in all three states found no commercial petroleum.

prot-083.title: The Warakurna large igneous province
prot-083.text: Central Australia was flooded with magma. The Warakurna large igneous province intruded the Giles Complex and Winburn granites and erupted the Bentley Supergroup volcanics. Those are bimodal volcanic rocks, widely considered comagmatic with the Giles Complex intrusions. The Palgrave Volcanic Association is a large volcanic and granite caldera edifice of about 1500 square kilometres. A link to the 1110 Ma African-Indian-Amazonian event is possible but unlikely.

prot-089.title: Proterocladus, the first multicellular green alga
prot-089.text:
Proterocladus antiquus, about 1 billion years old, is the first known preserved case of multicellularity in green algae. Around 1 Ga the first multicellular plants emerged, probably green algae, though the line between a colony and a multicellular organism is blurred. Proterocladus is known from the Nanfen and Diaoyutai Formations in China and the Svanbergfjellet Formation in Norway. Cell size and septa constrictions vary in P. antiquus, which casts doubt on every other Proterocladus species from Svanbergfjellet.

Why would going multicellular pay off? In lab studies of unicellular green algae, populations that grew into multicellular structures survived predation better.

prot-099.title: The Huainan worms
prot-099.text: Small worm-shaped organisms, visible to the eye, lived 840–740 Ma near Huainan City, Anhui, China. They record a transitional stage in evolution. Wang Guixiang and Sun Weiguo discovered them in the 1980s in Precambrian rock formations there. A similar biota about 1 billion years old was found on Russia's Timan Ridge. The Huainan biota has no jellyfish-like discs, as seen in the Ediacaran biota, and no forms close to sponges.

prot-105.title: The Pharusian Ocean opens and closes
prot-105.text: Rifting along the eastern margin of the West African craton during Rodinia's breakup opened the Pharusian Ocean about 800 Ma. It began to close about 730 Ma as the Tilemsi arc was subducted eastward against the Hoggar region. The western Hoggar massif is made of material from this ocean, including oceanic basalts, arc volcanic and sedimentary rocks. The Trans-Saharan Belt, running from Algeria to Benin, marks the suture zone of the closure.

prot-113.title: Shelled amoebae appear in the ice age
prot-113.text: Single-celled organisms with shells, testate amoebae (Arcellinida), first appear as fossils around 700 Ma in the Cryogenian. Arcellinid fossils date back even to the Tonian, around 789-759 million years ago. Porter (2000) suggests red and green algae, stramenopiles, ciliates and dinoflagellates also evolved in this period. Arcellinid testate amoebae are commonly found in soils, leaf litter, peat bogs and in or near fresh water.

prot-118.title: Songluo seaweeds in a break from the ice
prot-118.text: Seaweed grew during a pause in the ice age. Large macroalgae fossils of the Songluo Biota lived in South China around 650 Ma, during a short break in the Marinoan glaciation. It is the only known macrofossil biota from the Cryogenian, and the first large carbonaceous fossils in rocks of that age. Its shales and siltstones show no signs of glacial activity, and it was laid down on a distal shelf likely away from the margins of the large ice sheets. Macro-algae likely suffered a substantial extinction worldwide in the major glacial periods but persisted at less diverse numbers.

prot-122.title: Beardmore mountains rise in Antarctica
prot-122.text: The Beardmore orogeny built mountains in Antarctica from about 633 to 620 Ma. It reflects Rodinia's final breakup, as its fragments began moving together again toward Pannotia. Today it shows as an unconformity in the Transantarctic Mountains, between folded Late Proterozoic strata and overlying Early or Middle Cambrian sediments.

prot-125.title: The Timanide orogeny, Precambrian's last mountain belt
prot-125.text: The Timanide orogeny affected the northern Baltic Shield from about 620 to 550 Ma and is called the last major orogenic event of the Precambrian. Around 555 Ma Baltica's northern margin turned active, accreting the Timan-Pechora Basin, the northern Urals and Novaya Zemlya. Franz Josef Land and Kvitøya most likely joined Baltica in the same orogeny. The basement of Baltica's eastern margin is an Archaean craton and metamorphosed rocks at least 1.6 Ga old, ringed by the Timanide fold belt and overlain by Mesoproterozoic sediments.

prot-148.title: The Malagasy orogeny: India joins Africa
prot-148.text: India collided with Africa. In the Malagasy orogeny, from the Ediacaran into the Cambrian, India met an already joined Azania and Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block. It affected Madagascar, eastern East Africa and southern India about 550–515 Ma. Before that, the Mozambique Ocean had separated the Congo-Tanzania-Bangweulu Block of central Africa from Neoproterozoic India. The Betsimisaraka suture in eastern Madagascar has been identified as the boundary between the African and India terranes.

camb-007.title: Orthid brachiopods open their shells
camb-007.text: Orthida, an order of brachiopods, appeared in the Early Cambrian (Botomian) and became very diverse in Ordovician shelf seas. They began to differentiate in the late Early Cambrian and by the late Cambrian had diversified into many forms, 2–5 cm wide. Orthids are the oldest articulate brachiopods (Rhynchonelliformea), the order from which all other brachiopods of this group stem. They were sessile filter feeders, often anchoring themselves onto firm substrates.

camb-020.title: A carbon spike and two molluscs mark Stage 2
camb-020.text: A spike in carbon isotopes marks a boundary. The positive excursion, the ZHUCE, coincides with the first appearances of the molluscs Watsonella crosbyi and Aldanella attleborensis around 529 Ma. Together these markers reliably indicate the boundary between the Fortunian and Cambrian Stage 2. Stage 2 is the unnamed upper stage of the Terreneuvian Series, lying above the Fortunian and below Stage 3.

camb-022.title: Baltica collides with Arctida
camb-022.text: The Timanide Orogen formed as Baltica and Arctida collided between 528 and 510 Ma. Erosion of the mountain belt began in the Cambrian and grew stronger in the Ordovician. Sediments from it are found in the East European Platform, including the Cambrian Sablino Formation near Lake Ladoga. Not everyone accepts the collision: some researchers suggest there never was one.

camb-021.title: Ramgarh, an impact crater of uncertain age
camb-021.text: In 1972 A. R. Crawford proposed an impact origin for India's Ramgarh structure after finding shatter coned colluvium in the middle of the crater. A 2020 study gave stronger evidence, and the Earth Impact Database then classified it as a confirmed hypervelocity impact crater. Its age is less settled. Uranium–lead dating places the impact between 528 and 395 Ma, while other studies propose a younger age. Soft-sediment deformation near the apparent rim and an overlying diamictite layer suggest it struck a shallow-water environment.

camb-030.title: The Ritland crater, Norway
camb-030.text: A confirmed impact crater about 2 km across lies at Ritland, Norway, and formed about 520 ± 20 Ma. Geologist Fridtjof Riis first noticed it as a suspected crater in 2000. In 2008 came microscopic proof: shocked quartz particles, which form only under the very high pressures of 5-10 GPa in a meteorite impact.

camb-031.title: The Ross orogeny lifts the Transantarctic Mountains
camb-031.text: One of the most extensive mountain-building events in Antarctica, the Ross orogeny caused widespread plutonism and metamorphism. After early Cambrian rifting, Antarctica deformed and the Transantarctic Mountains rose in the mid-Cambrian. Bimodal magmatism and extension marked the start. Later, sedimentary rocks at the continental margin were deformed, metamorphosed and intruded with granite batholiths. From about 520 to 450 Ma, Cambrian sediments in the range were uplifted, folded, metamorphosed and intruded.

camb-042.title: Emu Bay Shale: muscle turned to mineral
camb-042.text: South Australia's Emu Bay Shale preserves soft tissue mineralized as apatite or calcium carbonate. It holds the oldest phosphatized muscle tissue and is younger than the Chengjiang and Sirius Passet Lagerstätten. It is dated to Stage 4, about 514–512 Ma. A 2023 study suggested about 512 million years, based on a correlation to a radiometric date of 511.87 ± 0.14 Ma in the contemporaneous Billy Creek Formation. In 2011, paired compound eyes 2-3 centimetres long from the shale were described and assigned to Anomalocaris.

camb-041.title: The Delamerian orogeny folds South Australia
camb-041.text: The Delamerian orogeny, about 514 to 490 Ma, ended deposition in the Adelaide Superbasin and folded and deformed its rocks. Australia's eastern margin was inverted and became a subduction zone of the Palaeo-Pacific. Most rocks of the Kanmantoo Province were highly deformed and underwent moderate to high grade metamorphism. The event is named after Delamere, a small town on the Fleurieu Peninsula where evidence for it was found. One list of orogenies gives a shorter span.

camb-053.title: The Glikson crater, Western Australia
camb-053.text: The Glikson crater in Western Australia is about 19 km across. Shatter cones and microscopic shock effects are reliable evidence of an impact. Nearby dolerite dated 508 ± 5 Ma suggests the impact is younger, probably Paleozoic. A ring-shaped aeromagnetic anomaly at the site was probably caused by the impact disrupting a horizontal sill of magnetic igneous rock.

camb-058.title: Conodonts: teeth that lasted 300 million years
camb-058.text:
Conodonts, eel-like jawless animals, are known mostly from their teeth. They first appear in the Middle Cambrian and lasted more than 300 million years, from the Cambrian to the start of the Jurassic. The hard, mineralised tooth-like structures called conodont elements sat in the oral cavity in life and were used to process food. It has been proposed that conodonts may be stem-cyclostomes, more closely related to hagfish and lampreys than to jawed vertebrates.

They diversified extensively in the early Ordovician, peaked in the middle of that period, and declined sharply in the late Ordovician and Silurian. Sources differ on when they began: some say about 520 Ma, others the late Cambrian.

camb-060.title: The Paleo-Tethys Ocean begins to open
camb-060.text:
The Paleo-Tethys Ocean began to open along Gondwana's northern margin in the Middle Cambrian. It grew through the Paleozoic and closed in the Late Triassic, lasting about 400 million years. It was a precursor to the Tethys Ocean (Neo-Tethys), which lay between Gondwana and the Hunic terranes, continental fragments that broke off Gondwana and moved north.

A last remnant of the Paleo-Tethys might be oceanic crust under the Black Sea. Its role in the supercontinent cycle, especially the break-up of Pangaea, is unresolved.

camb-061.title: Paradoxides, the giant trilobites
camb-061.text: Paradoxides, a genus of large to very large trilobites, lived throughout the world in the Middle Cambrian (Miaolingian). They were the largest Cambrian trilobites. One record-breaking specimen of Paradoxides davidis, described by John William Salter in 1863, is 37 cm long. Like many early trilobites, Paradoxides had nonfulcrate thorax segments that allowed the animal to roll up.

camb-070.title: The Gardnos impact hits a shallow sea
camb-070.text: A meteorite 200–300 m across struck Buskerud, Norway, about 500 ± 10 Ma and left the 5 km Gardnos crater. Post-impact sediments show it hit a shallow sea, and rock avalanches and debris flows followed when the crater rim was breached. The impact fractured the bedrock and forced a powder of crushed rock into all the fractures, forming an impact breccia. The site was first believed to be a volcanic crater, but in 1990 geologists Johan Naterstad and Johannes A. Dons confirmed a meteorite impact.

camb-071.title: The Mizarai crater, Lithuania
camb-071.text: The 5 km Mizarai crater in Lithuania formed about 500 Ma, though sources give the uncertainty as ±10 or ±20 Ma. It is the second largest in the country and is not exposed at the surface; the village of Mizarai now stands on the site. Gediminas Motuza discovered it during the international Eurobridge seismic survey, which reached depths of 90-100 km.

camb-073.title: Orsten: microscopic animals of the seafloor
camb-073.text: Sweden's Kinnekulle Orsten and Alum Shale reveal the oldest well-documented seafloor meiofauna, including microscopic arthropods such as free-living pentastomids. The Orsten fauna are fossilized organisms preserved in Cambrian rocks (Late Miaolingian to Furongian), notably at Kinnekulle and on the island of Oland. Such deposits belong to the Konservat-Lagerstatten, known for exceptional preservation of fossilized organisms or traces. This one dates to about 500 Ma.
